title: Learning from a teacher
tomorrow: dying, the Buddha named no successor. so who teaches now?

lines: THE HALF-SECOND BEFORE YOUR HAND GOES UP.
A CALM MONK ON THE STREET.
cards: The half-second before your hand goes up in class can feel like stepping off a ledge.
Sariputta was already a serious seeker, a wanderer studying under another teacher, when he saw a monk named Assaji walking the street on his alms round.
Something in the way he walked, calm, eyes lowered, unhurried, stopped Sariputta cold. If anyone has found the way, he thought, it's this one. But he didn't interrupt.
He followed at a distance and waited until the alms round was done. Then he asked: who is your teacher, and what does he teach?

teach.b: Assaji's answer is the surprise. I'm new, he says. I've only just gone forth.
I can't teach it to you in detail, but I can tell you the meaning briefly.

teach.h: ONE VERSE: A CAUSE, AND ITS ENDING.
teach.b: Then he gives one short verse: of the things that arise from a cause, the Tathagata has told the cause, and also how they cease. That's all. A beginner, honest about being a beginner, with one line.
And the Vinaya says that on hearing it, the eye of the teaching opened in Sariputta.

teach.h: MOGGALLANA SEES IT IN HIS FACE.
teach.b: He went straight to his friend Moggallana, who saw it in his face before he said a word, and the two of them went to the Buddha. Look at what the story keeps. A seeker who waits for the right moment instead of barging in.
A question asked plainly. A teacher who says what he doesn't know.
That's why asking is built into Buddhist learning: students bring questions to their teachers, lay people bring them to monks, and suttas open with questions, like the Kalamas' and Ananda's.

teach.h: A TEACHER IS SOMEONE YOU ASK.
teach.b: A teacher isn't only someone who talks.
A teacher is someone you ask. On Thursday, Mai has a question for the visitor.

how: Buddhists bring questions to teachers at talks, retreats and temple visits, often in a set question-and-answer time; in many monasteries a student requests an interview with a teacher to ask about their practice.

games.q: what does “learning from a teacher” mean?
o: serving a teacher for years before you're allowed to speak
asking a teacher plainly, at the right moment, and listening
copying a teacher's sayings until you know them all by heart

games.q: the question on the street — tap the pairs.
p: a seeker who waited, then asked
things from a cause, and how they cease
saw the change in his friend's face

s: Assaji gave Sariputta a long, detailed teaching
he said he was new and gave the meaning in one short verse.
Sariputta interrupted Assaji's alms round to ask
he followed at a distance and waited until the round was done.
Moggallana saw the change in Sariputta before he spoke
he saw it in his friend's face, and they went to the Buddha together.

games.q: at a temple open day, the abbot is greeting a long line of guests. you have a real question about your meditation. what fits the Sariputta story?
o: wait till the line clears, then ask it plainly and briefly
skip it; a busy teacher's time is for students further along
ask a friend instead, since any answer is as good as his
games.why: Sariputta didn't interrupt the alms round, and he didn't skip the question either. he waited for the moment, then asked plainly.

practice: Think of one question you've been carrying, about practice, about life, about something someone said. Say it out loud once, plainly, the way Sariputta did, as if to someone who might know.
Then sit, and let it hang in the air without hurrying an answer.

wordCard.voice: Learning from a teacher: waiting for the right moment, asking plainly, and listening even when the answer is short.

orig.note: Pali: a question, the kind put to a teacher.

carryVoice: Here's your line: ask, because a teacher is someone you ask. Nineteen days in, still asking.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.23 (Sariputta meets Assaji)
